symptom_description: A motor-drive controller intermittently reports overcurrent during high-duty operation even though the motor continues running normally. The event occurs most often at duty cycles above roughly 70% and appears as one or two high current samples near a PWM transition. Lower-duty operation is stable, and the trip is not consistently associated with an increase in commanded torque.

likely_causes.cause_description: The current-sense amplifier and input filter have not settled from the PWM-edge transient when the ADC samples, causing a switching artifact to be interpreted as motor current.
implicated_modules: PWM timing and ADC trigger logic
likely_causes.failure_mechanism: The PWM transition can create a fast common-mode or ground disturbance at the low-side shunt and amplifier inputs. The amplifier output shows a transient recovery, and the ADC trigger occurs before that observed recovery is complete. The filter adds a time constant of about 2.2 microseconds, so the signal at the ADC pin may also still be moving at the 0.7-microsecond sampling point. The resulting elevated conversion can cross the software threshold even when motor current has not increased.
likely_causes.supporting_evidence: The reported ADC spikes are brief and edge-aligned, the independent current probe does not show a corresponding current increase, and the amplifier output has a PWM-synchronized overshoot lasting longer than the delay to sampling. The high-duty dependence is consistent with a narrower or less favorable quiet sampling window, though the ADC-pin waveform has not yet been measured.
predicted_measurement_signatures: The ADC-pin voltage will still be recovering at the current sampling instant and will be higher than its settled value during affected cycles.
Moving the ADC trigger later into a quiet interval, while keeping motor operating conditions comparable, will reduce the reported spikes.
The amplifier output or ADC-pin transient will track PWM edges more closely than the current probe waveform.

likely_causes.cause_description: The ADC sample-and-hold is being disturbed by the filtered amplifier source or by the voltage retained from a preceding conversion.
implicated_modules: ADC channel sequence and acquisition timing
likely_causes.failure_mechanism: The 1.0 kΩ series resistance can limit how quickly the ADC input capacitance is replenished during acquisition. If the acquisition interval is short or another channel was previously at a different voltage, the sampling capacitor can pull the input away from its true value and produce a conversion dependent on channel order or acquisition time. PWM-edge recovery may make this effect more apparent in the affected phase of the cycle.
likely_causes.supporting_evidence: The ADC input uses a series resistor and the voltage at the ADC pin has not been observed. The amplifier transient and early trigger already provide a stronger explanation, but the source impedance and channel sequence are unspecified and should be tested before excluding acquisition error.
predicted_measurement_signatures: The error will depend on ADC acquisition time or on the voltage of the previously converted channel.
A longer acquisition interval or a buffer with suitable settling behavior will reduce the error even when the PWM trigger phase is unchanged.
The amplifier output may have settled while the ADC pin or conversion code remains sensitive to channel sequence.

likely_causes.cause_description: A real short-duration shunt-current transient is being missed or attenuated by the independent motor-lead current measurement.
likely_causes.failure_mechanism: A fast current change through the shunt could be narrower than the current probe response or could differ from the motor-lead current at the relevant instant because of current paths within the power stage. Such a shunt event could produce a real voltage increase that the ADC captures while the external probe does not resolve.
likely_causes.supporting_evidence: The independent probe does not show a corresponding pulse, which weakens this explanation, but its bandwidth and exact measurement point are not specified. A direct, bandwidth-adequate differential measurement across the shunt is needed before treating the ADC reading as purely an artifact.
predicted_measurement_signatures: A high-bandwidth differential measurement across the shunt will show a current-proportional pulse aligned with the reported high samples if the transient is real.
The event magnitude will scale with load or switching conditions in a way consistent with actual phase or bus current rather than only with the ADC trigger delay.
Changing the sampling instant without changing the power-stage waveform will change which part of a real pulse is captured, but will not remove the pulse from the shunt waveform.

design_conditions: The drive uses a low-side 10 mΩ shunt, a current-sense amplifier with nominal gain of 20, and a single-ended ADC input. A 1.0 kΩ series resistor and 2.2 nF capacitor form the ADC input filter. The controller schedules one current conversion per PWM cycle and samples 0.7 microseconds after the switching edge. The overcurrent limit is evaluated directly from the converted sample. The observed behavior occurs at high duty cycle with the normal motor and gate-drive configuration; the current probe is installed on the motor lead.

verification_plan.procedure: With the motor operating at a repeatable high-duty condition, capture the shunt differential voltage, amplifier output, ADC-pin voltage, PWM edge, and ADC trigger using a common time base and suitable probe bandwidth. Confirm the measurement does not materially load the analog nodes.
verification_plan.expected_outcome: The leading diagnosis predicts that the amplifier output and/or ADC-pin voltage is still recovering at the current 0.7-microsecond sampling instant, without a matching current pulse on the shunt waveform.
verification_plan.interpretation: A confirmed shunt pulse redirects the investigation to the power stage and current-limit response. A settled ADC pin with an anomalous code shifts attention toward acquisition settings, channel sequencing, ADC reference, or digital conversion handling.

verification_plan.procedure: Determine a sampling point after the measured analog recovery interval and within a repeatable quiet part of the PWM cycle. Update the trigger timing, then validate that the selected point remains valid across the intended duty-cycle range.
verification_plan.expected_outcome: The ADC codes should agree with the independent current measurement and should no longer contain edge-correlated excursions that cause false overcurrent decisions.
verification_plan.interpretation: If errors remain, do not mask them by raising the overcurrent threshold; inspect ADC acquisition behavior and the input RC network, then verify whether the shunt waveform contains a real transient.

verification_plan.procedure: At the selected timing, exercise the drive across its specified duty cycle, load, supply, and temperature range while recording current readings and overcurrent flags. Compare the measured peak current against the existing protection limit and confirm protection still responds to a controlled genuine current increase.
verification_plan.expected_outcome: Normal operation should produce stable readings without false trips, while a genuine current-limit condition should still be detected within the required response time.
verification_plan.interpretation: Any residual edge-correlated error calls for additional front-end or timing refinement. Failure to detect a genuine overcurrent after the change indicates that the trigger adjustment or filtering has compromised protection and must be revised.

diagnostic_summary: The leading diagnosis is that the ADC samples the low-side current-sense path before its PWM-edge transient has settled. The amplifier overshoot lasts longer than the 0.7-microsecond trigger delay, and the ADC input filter adds further settling time, while the independent current measurement does not corroborate the reported peaks. Capture the shunt and ADC-pin waveforms together, then move sampling to a verified quiet interval and validate both false-trip immunity and real overcurrent response.

discriminating_tests.test_description: Sweep the ADC trigger delay across the PWM period while holding duty cycle and load as constant as practical. Record the amplifier output, ADC-pin voltage, conversion code, and a bandwidth-adequate differential shunt waveform on a common time base.
discriminating_tests.target_signal_or_module: Current-sense amplifier output, ADC pin, shunt voltage, and PWM trigger timing
discriminating_tests.expected_results: If the leading cause is incomplete analog settling, the code spikes will be largest near the PWM edge and fall when sampling is delayed until the amplifier and ADC pin settle. If a real current pulse is present, it will remain visible on the shunt waveform even when the ADC trigger is moved.
discriminating_tests.diagnostic_interpretation: An edge-dependent ADC error without a matching shunt pulse supports a sampling-phase or analog-recovery diagnosis. A shunt pulse proportional to current supports a power-stage transient and requires current-limit evaluation against the actual waveform.

discriminating_tests.test_description: Keep the PWM phase fixed and vary the ADC acquisition interval; then repeat with the preceding ADC channel set first to a low voltage and then to a high voltage.
discriminating_tests.target_signal_or_module: ADC acquisition timing, channel sequence, and ADC input node
discriminating_tests.expected_results: A sample-and-hold settling error will change with acquisition interval or preceding-channel voltage. A front-end recovery transient will primarily follow the PWM edge and may remain even when acquisition time is lengthened, while a real current pulse will remain visible across the shunt measurement.
discriminating_tests.diagnostic_interpretation: Strong dependence on acquisition time or channel order identifies an ADC drive or sequencing contribution. Dependence mainly on PWM phase points to amplifier or filter recovery; a corroborated shunt pulse points to a real power-stage event.

discriminating_tests.test_description: Temporarily move the ADC trigger to a measured quiet portion of the PWM cycle without changing the amplifier, filter, threshold, or power stage, and compare reported current with the independent current measurement.
discriminating_tests.target_signal_or_module: PWM-to-ADC trigger timing and current conversion path
discriminating_tests.expected_results: If the false trips arise from switching transients at the original aperture, the high codes and overcurrent flags should disappear or substantially decrease at the quiet sampling point while the independently measured current remains similar.
discriminating_tests.diagnostic_interpretation: A clean result supports timing-related contamination but does not by itself distinguish amplifier recovery from ADC acquisition error. Persistent high readings require checking the ADC-pin waveform, channel history, and direct shunt measurement.

cross_module_reasoning: The shunt converts power-stage current into a small differential voltage; the current-sense amplifier and RC network condition that voltage before the ADC samples it, and firmware applies the overcurrent threshold to the converted result. The independent motor-lead measurement does not corroborate the reported peak, while the amplifier overshoot persists beyond the current ADC trigger delay. This points first to an analog settling or sampling-phase problem rather than a sustained increase in motor current. The RC network can further delay settling at the ADC pin, and the sample-and-hold may introduce an additional channel-history effect. A direct shunt measurement is still necessary because the external probe's bandwidth and placement are not established.
measurement_observations: The current channel normally reports about 1.8 to 2.1 A. During an event, the ADC-derived value reaches 3.4 to 3.8 A for one or two samples, above a 3.0 A software limit. A separate current probe shows approximately 2.0 A at the same time, with no corresponding current pulse at its measurement bandwidth. The current-sense amplifier output has a brief overshoot after a PWM edge and returns close to its prior level in about 1.2 microseconds. The ADC trigger is currently 0.7 microseconds after that edge. No simultaneous measurement at the ADC pin has been made.

likely_causes.cause_description: Dynamic disturbance of the ADC reference or its local return during controller SPI activity is the leading cause of the positive code steps.
implicated_modules: ADC reference buffer and decoupling network
likely_causes.failure_mechanism: SPI switching current can disturb the reference buffer output or create a transient between the reference and ADC ground. Because SAR output code scales approximately with input voltage divided by reference voltage, a short reduction in VREF produces a positive code shift even if the analog input is steady. The measured 14 mV reference dip is of the right sign and approximate magnitude to explain a shift near 0.5% at midscale.
likely_causes.supporting_evidence: The code steps are synchronized with SPI activity, the measured reference dip has the polarity that increases ADC codes, and the instrumentation-amplifier output is nearly unchanged. The shared return and reference network provide a plausible coupling path. Bridge-excitation transients remain an alternative because they have not been captured with sufficient bandwidth.
predicted_measurement_signatures: A low-noise DC source held at the ADC input will show a similar code increase during SPI bursts if the reference or ADC ground is responsible.
The code error will track the magnitude and timing of the VREF-to-ADC-ground transient.
Reducing SPI edge activity or improving reference isolation and local decoupling will reduce the code step without changing the bridge signal.

likely_causes.cause_description: SPI-related disturbance of bridge excitation or bridge return is changing the differential signal before it reaches the ADC.
likely_causes.failure_mechanism: Controller switching current can couple through a shared supply or return path into the bridge. An excitation change can alter the bridge differential output, while a return shift can appear as a differential or common-mode disturbance at the instrumentation-amplifier inputs. Either effect can propagate through the amplifier and produce a code change that happens to coincide with SPI activity.
likely_causes.supporting_evidence: The bridge and controller share the board, and the bridge excitation has only been checked with a handheld meter, which would not reveal a short transient. This cause is weakened by the nearly steady amplifier output and the directly observed VREF dip, but it is not excluded until excitation and input nodes are captured with suitable bandwidth.
predicted_measurement_signatures: A differential measurement across the bridge or a high-bandwidth capture of its excitation will show a transient synchronized with SPI bursts if this cause is present.
Replacing the bridge temporarily with a stable differential input at the amplifier will remove the error if the disturbance originates in the bridge or its excitation.
A stable input applied directly to the ADC will remain stable if the ADC reference and ground are not independently disturbed.

likely_causes.cause_description: ADC input acquisition settling is insufficient under the active sampling and channel-switching sequence.
likely_causes.failure_mechanism: If the ADC input driver or its filter cannot settle the sampling capacitor within the acquisition interval, conversion codes can depend on the preceding channel or sampling event. SPI activity could be correlated with the sequence that triggers the error, although it would not by itself explain the measured reference dip.
likely_causes.supporting_evidence: The ADC is a SAR converter, so its input drive and acquisition timing merit verification. No source-impedance or channel-order sweep has been reported. The stable amplifier output and observed VREF disturbance make this less likely than a reference-related cause.
predicted_measurement_signatures: The error will vary with ADC acquisition time, sample rate, or the voltage on the previously selected channel.
A longer acquisition interval or a buffer placed close to the ADC will reduce the error even if SPI traffic is unchanged.
The code error will not consistently scale with the measured VREF dip if acquisition settling is the dominant cause.

design_conditions: A 350-ohm full bridge is excited from 3.3 V and read through an instrumentation amplifier whose output is biased near midscale. The amplifier drives a 16-bit SAR ADC using a nominal 3.0 V external reference. The reference reaches the ADC through a series resistor and has local decoupling at the converter. The controller samples at 2 kS/s and runs 8 MHz SPI bursts on the same board. The ADC, reference buffer, and controller return through a shared ground region. Measurements were taken with the board at room temperature and the sensor mechanically undisturbed.

verification_plan.procedure: Reproduce the fault with the sensor stationary and record synchronized traces of ADC input, VREF relative to ADC ground, bridge excitation, SPI activity, and converted codes using probes and bandwidth adequate for the observed transient.
verification_plan.expected_outcome: The leading diagnosis predicts that the reference-to-ground transient coincides with the code shift while the amplifier output remains comparatively steady.
verification_plan.interpretation: If the bridge or amplifier signal moves first and sufficiently to explain the codes, investigate that upstream path before changing the reference network. If no analog node explains the error, revisit ADC timing and digital data handling.

verification_plan.procedure: With the fault source localized to the reference path, make a controlled change that reduces reference-path impedance or isolates reference and digital return currents, following the reference buffer and ADC requirements. Change one element at a time and retain the original configuration for comparison.
verification_plan.expected_outcome: The VREF-to-ground transient and associated code step should both decrease when the effective coupling or reference impedance is reduced.
verification_plan.interpretation: If VREF improves but the code step does not, the reference transient is not the sole cause; check ADC ground, acquisition settling, and bridge excitation. If neither improves, the chosen change did not address the coupling path.

verification_plan.procedure: Repeat quiet and SPI-active acquisition over the intended sampling rate, SPI activity range, supply range, and operating temperature, then compare the residual error with the system measurement-error budget.
verification_plan.expected_outcome: The corrected system should meet its measurement-error limit without code steps correlated with SPI bursts, and the reference should remain within its specified transient tolerance.
verification_plan.interpretation: A remaining activity-correlated error indicates an unresolved coupling path or a second cause. A clean result across the operating envelope supports the diagnosis and the corrective change.

diagnostic_summary: The leading diagnosis is SPI-correlated disturbance of the ADC reference-to-ground path: the measured VREF dip has the correct polarity and approximate magnitude to explain the positive midscale code shift, while the instrumentation-amplifier output remains nearly steady. Confirm the result with a stable ADC input and synchronized measurements of the reference, bridge excitation, and analog signal before changing the reference or return network.
symptom_description: A 16-bit bridge-measurement channel reports brief positive steps in the inferred sensor value whenever the controller performs a burst of SPI traffic. The steps begin within one sample of the burst and disappear within several samples afterward. They are reproducible at room temperature with a stationary sensor and do not occur during quiet acquisition intervals.

discriminating_tests.test_description: Replace the bridge-amplifier signal temporarily with a stable low-noise DC source near 1.50 V, preserve the normal ADC timing, and alternate quiet intervals with the same SPI bursts. Capture VREF and ADC ground differentially at the converter pins.
discriminating_tests.target_signal_or_module: ADC input, VREF-to-ADC-ground voltage, and controller SPI activity
discriminating_tests.expected_results: If the reference or ADC return is responsible, the code step should persist with the stable input and coincide with a VREF-to-ground transient. If bridge excitation or the bridge input path is responsible, the step should largely disappear while the stable source is connected.
discriminating_tests.diagnostic_interpretation: Persistence with the stable source prioritizes the reference, ground, or ADC path. Disappearance shifts priority to bridge excitation, bridge return, or the instrumentation-amplifier input path.

discriminating_tests.test_description: Capture bridge excitation, differential bridge output, instrumentation-amplifier output, and ADC reference during the same SPI burst using appropriately rated differential probes and a common time base.
discriminating_tests.target_signal_or_module: Bridge excitation and output, instrumentation-amplifier output, and ADC reference network
discriminating_tests.expected_results: A bridge-originated disturbance will appear first in excitation or bridge differential voltage and then propagate to the amplifier output. A reference-originated disturbance will appear at VREF while the bridge and amplifier output remain substantially steady.
discriminating_tests.diagnostic_interpretation: The earliest correlated disturbance identifies the likely entry point. If both paths move, compare their timing and predicted contribution to determine whether one is dominant or both contribute.

discriminating_tests.test_description: Repeat the measurement while increasing the ADC acquisition interval and varying the preceding channel voltage, without changing the SPI burst pattern.
discriminating_tests.target_signal_or_module: ADC sample-and-hold input and channel sequencing
discriminating_tests.expected_results: A settling problem should decrease with a longer acquisition interval and should vary with the preceding channel. A reference disturbance should remain correlated with the VREF transient and SPI activity despite the timing change.
discriminating_tests.diagnostic_interpretation: A strong acquisition-time or channel-order dependence supports an input-settling contribution; little change alongside a persistent VREF-correlated error weakens it.

cross_module_reasoning: The sensor bridge and instrumentation amplifier form the analog input path, while the SAR ADC converts that signal relative to its reference and the controller creates bursty digital switching current. The amplifier output measurement argues against a large disturbance originating upstream of the ADC, whereas the reference-pin capture reveals a transient coincident with the code shift. A lower reference makes a fixed midscale input occupy a larger fraction of full scale, which predicts the observed positive code direction. The shared return offers a plausible path from SPI activity into the reference-to-ADC-ground relationship. Bridge excitation remains a secondary possibility because its fast transient response has not been measured, and an acquisition-timing issue should be checked if the reference transient does not account for the full error.
measurement_observations: At a nominal ADC input of about 1.50 V, the recorded code rises by approximately 150 to 190 counts during SPI bursts, corresponding to roughly 0.5% of midscale. A differential probe at the ADC reference pins shows VREF falling from 3.000 V to about 2.986 V for 20 to 40 microseconds, synchronized with the code increase. The instrumentation-amplifier output remains within 0.2 mV of its quiet value during the observed events. Bridge excitation remains near 3.30 V on a handheld meter; its transient behavior has not yet been captured with an oscilloscope.
